metadata.title: ExoColumn: a one-dimensional radiative-convective equilibrium model for planetary atmospheres
metadata.description:
ExoColumn is a one-dimensional radiative–convective equilibrium (RCE) model for planetary atmospheres, built directly on the ExoRT correlated-k radiative transfer code that also serves as the radiation core of the ExoCAM three-dimensional model. ExoColumn time-marches a single atmospheric column to radiative–convective equilibrium by calling ExoRT's aerad_driver each step, with a prognostic surface slab, surface turbulent fluxes, moist convection, condensation, and a stratospheric cold-trap closure.

ExoColumn couples an independently developed atmospheric column physics package to ExoRT without modifying it, so that spectroscopic updates propagate from ExoRT to ExoColumn automatically. The model reproduces present-day Earth to within a few kelvin of independent RCE codes, and reproduces the inner-edge (moist- and runaway-greenhouse) and outer-edge (maximum-greenhouse) habitable-zone limits of the Clima model lineage, extended to twelve host stars spanning 2000–7200 K and to planetary masses of 0.1, 1, and 5 Earth masses.

This release accompanies the paper “Validation of Habitable Zone Limits with a New Radiative-Convective Equilibrium Climate Model” (Haqq-Misra, Wolf & Kopparapu). The reference/ directory contains self-contained validation and habitable-zone cases, each with the data and plotting script that regenerate the corresponding published figure.

metadata.title: SpriteOptics
metadata.description: SpriteOptics v1.0 is a scientific software developed in Python for the post-processing of numerical simulations of atmospheric sprite streamer electrical discharges. The program processes VTK files containing electric field and electron density information and estimates synthetic optical signals corresponding to N₂ emissions at 337 nm, LBH, and O₂ at 777.4 nm. It incorporates reduced electric field (E/N) calculation, E/N-dependent excitation coefficients, QSS approximation, collisional quenching, atmospheric attenuation, axisymmetric volumetric reconstruction, source-observer geometry, and configurable field-of-view selection. The results are generated as time series of modeled irradiance and exported in CSV and graphical formats.

metadata.title: MELITE — Multi-Model Classifier Evaluator
metadata.description:
v0.3.0 (2026-08-28)

MELITE is a pre-stable comparative classifier evaluator for tabular classification, classifier selection with nested cross-validation, final model export, and artifact-based inference. It operates at the tabular modeling level by consuming numeric feature matrices and labels. MELITE evaluates SVC, Random Forest, XGBoost, and opt-in Stacking classifiers under an outer repeated-stratified cross-validation framework. Tunable classifiers are optimized with Optuna inside each outer training split, under the same declared trial budget across tunable classifiers. It selects the best active classifier by mean outer-CV F1-macro, persists aggregate and per-fold evaluation evidence together with per-search optimization evidence, and supports final model retraining, export, and artifact-based inference.

metadata.title: hsjwang/solutions-table: Cyber Security Card Game V 1.0
metadata.description:
Release notes v1.0.0 — first public release

The Solutions dimension for the University of Washington Security Cards, with a browser implementation, facilitator materials, and a ten-scenario library.

The original toolkit stops deliberately at threat discovery. This adds the other half of the professional task — choosing proportionate controls under a budget and being able to defend the choice — and the gameplay that makes it cost something.

The deck 21 control cards mapped to CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1 at the level of individual safeguards, not control titles. A card reading only "CIS Control 6" tells a novice nothing; naming 6.1 and 6.2 tells them what the control actually asks an organization to do. Cost derived from CIS Implementation Group, not designer judgment. 1 point is essential hygiene; 3 points need staff and money. Cost is difficulty, not usefulness. 7 modifier cards carrying principles rather than controls — defense in depth, fail-safe defaults, least privilege, human factors, risk acceptance, compensating control, deferred investment. Free, but each demands a specific spoken justification or it returns to the deck. 4 optional inject cards for facilitator-introduced adversity. Card set determined by a coverage analysis against Implementation Group 1, which found five foundational gaps in our earlier fifteen-card deck: asset inventory, software inventory, secure configuration, email and browser protections, and incident response planning. The game Three-phase core loop. Build a threat model from four cards and place it on a 3×3 grid; list recommended measures and spend a budget; re-place the threat and say what still gets through. The pre/post delta is both the lesson and a measurable artifact. Budget calibrated against expected hand value. Six points buys about half a typical hand. The earlier figure of ten bought 82%, which is not a constraint. Deals guarantee an answerable threat. Every hand contains at least one card that addresses the drawn threat, and by default all teams get the same eight. Campaign play across a term: coverage against the scenario's expert key decides whether a threat eases, holds, or drifts; a threat left at Very Likely realizes, with the outcome settled by earlier purchases rather than by chance. Standing risks (optional): two problems the client already had, competing for the same budget, so that a control touching several problems outscores one that only touches today's incident. The application Multiplayer over Firebase Realtime Database. Facilitator, player and projector views from one URL. Role and seat ownership enforced by database rules, not by the interface — a student cannot become facilitator or edit another team's board. The role frees itself two minutes after the holder's last action so a dead laptop does not strand a class. Phase guidance in the interface: what to do, the one thing that matters, and what done looks like. Per-card feedback at Phase 3. Every purchase is shown against the threat with a written reason — 52 justifications across the ten scenarios — rather than a bare verdict. Withheld until Phase 3 so teams cannot shop by watching what lights up. Control condition built in. Removes Solutions cards and the budget and changes nothing else. Stored in the session, locked once play starts. CSV export covering the measures a study needs. Accessibility: WCAG AA contrast in both light and dark themes, a text-size control, 12.5px minimum type, visible focus rings, and no reliance on colour alone. Materials 27-page facilitator manual, including intervention guidance, an assessment rubric, campaign play, the controlled-study protocol, and Appendix C: ten scenarios with expert keys and debrief questions. 4-page quick reference, printable as one folded sheet. 8-page survey instrument with participant and facilitator forms, plus Qualtrics import files. Known limits The board polls rather than pushes; four seconds by default. One device drives per team. No accounts — appropriate for a classroom, not for real client data. The four original Security Cards dimensions ship as placeholders; the UW deck is copyrighted by its authors. Whether a purpose-built interface preserves the discussion that physical cards produce is unmeasured. Status of the evidence

A formative study with 19 multidisciplinary participants established feasibility and accessibility and produced the design requirements this version answers. It does not establish learning gains, and this deck has not yet been played in a classroom. A controlled evaluation is scheduled, and the accompanying paper reports its design. Please treat the artifact as a designed and documented proposal rather than a validated intervention.

Upgrading

First release; nothing to upgrade from. If you cloned during development, note that the Firebase config moved back into src/backend.js as literals — the build-time environment variables were removed after an empty repository secret silently overrode them and produced a site that loaded and then refused every write.

metadata.title: HBB2OBB: Horizontal to Oriented Bounding Box Conversion and Evaluation Tool
metadata.description:
HBB2OBB converts horizontal (axis-aligned) bounding boxes (HBBs) into oriented (rotated) bounding boxes (OBBs) by using existing HBB annotations as prompts for segmentation models from the SAM (Segment Anything Model) family. It targets object detection tasks where objects appear at arbitrary orientations, such as aerial imagery, satellite data, and traffic monitoring, producing oriented boxes that tightly encapsulate non-upright objects without any re-annotation. Beyond conversion, it provides evaluation, hyperparameter optimization, and annotation format-conversion tools, exposed through both a command-line interface and a Python API.

Why HBB2OBB

  • 🎯 Accurate OBBs from HBBs: prompts SAM-family segmentation models with existing horizontal boxes to fit tight oriented boxes around non-upright objects, with no re-annotation required.
  • 🧩 Model ensemble: combines masks from multiple SAM variants through majority voting for more robust, accurate results.
  • 🛡️ Spatially constrained and safe: region-specific masking and contour refinement keep segmentation inside the object, and a fallback retains the original HBB when no valid mask is found.
  • 🔎 Confidence-scored output: every OBB receives a heuristic quality score in [0, 1] that flags silent fallbacks and low-confidence conversions, so you know which boxes to trust; the detector's own confidence can be carried through instead of, or on top of, that score.
  • 📐 Flexible scaling: positive or negative scale factors, optionally different for the short and long sides, recover cropped object parts or tighten overly conservative annotations.
  • 📊 Evaluate and optimize: built-in IoU evaluation against ground truth plus a hyperparameter optimizer over SAM inference resolution and scale factors.
  • 🔄 Format conversions: utilities to move between YOLO TXT and COCO, Pascal VOC, and LabelMe JSON annotations.

Features

  • HBB to OBB conversion of YOLO-format annotations using SAM-based segmentation.
  • Multiple model support: SAM, SAM2, SAM2.1, SAM3, Mobile SAM, and FastSAM families.
  • Model ensemble via majority voting for enhanced accuracy.
  • Confidence scoring: a per-OBB quality score flags silent fallbacks and low-confidence conversions for triage, optionally combined with the detector confidence from the input.
  • Polygon output: optionally save the segmentation contour behind each OBB, row-aligned with the OBB file, as a tighter object outline for downstream masking.
  • Evaluation tools to assess OBB accuracy against ground truth using IoU metrics.
  • Hyperparameter optimization over SAM inference resolutions and HBB scale factors.
  • Visualization tools for HBBs, segmentation masks, derived contours, and resulting OBBs.
  • Format conversion utilities between LabelMe, COCO, and Pascal VOC annotations and YOLO TXT.

Planned Enhancements

  • Improved morphological operations for better mask refinement.
  • Integration with popular object detection libraries to alleviate the need for HBB annotations.
  • Support for additional segmentation models beyond the SAM and FastSAM families.

Related Projects

  • Geo-trax 🛰️: georeferenced vehicle trajectory extraction pipeline for high-altitude drone imagery. Its vehicle detector produces the horizontal bounding box annotations HBB2OBB consumes, so it can supply the HBB inputs for vehicle use cases (car, bus, truck, and motorcycle).
  • Stabilo 🌀: Python library for video and trajectory stabilization using robust homography transformations, supporting various feature detectors, RANSAC algorithms, and user-defined masks.
  • Stabilo-Optimize 🎯: benchmarking and hyperparameter optimization framework for Stabilo, evaluating stabilization performance through ground-truth-free assessment using random perturbations.

Citation

If you use HBB2OBB in your research or software, please cite the archived release:

@software{fonod2026hbb2obb,
  author  = {Fonod, Robert},
  title   = {HBB2OBB: Horizontal to Oriented Bounding Box Conversion and Evaluation Tool},
  year    = {2026},
  license = {MIT},
  doi     = {10.5281/zenodo.15151143},
  url     = {https://github.com/rfonod/hbb2obb}
}

Contributions

Community contributions are welcome: open a GitHub Issue or submit a pull request.

metadata.title: Emotion detection in short texts using deep learning and decision threshold optimization with differential evolution: Reproducibility Package
metadata.description:
Emotion-Classification: Experimental Code and Supporting Materials

This repository contains the experimental code and supporting materials used for emotion classification experiments on Spanish tweets. The resource is intended to facilitate the reproducibility of the methodology, data-processing workflow, model evaluation, and statistical analysis described in the associated research article.

The repository provides Python-based scripts covering the main stages of the experimental workflow, including tweet corpus preprocessing, feature extraction and vectorization, model training and evaluation, classification analysis, carbon-emission estimation, and statistical significance analysis.

Repository contents

The repository is organized into the following directories:

  • Corpus_Tweets/ — Scripts and resources associated with corpus preprocessing.

  • Characteristics/ — Scripts for feature extraction and vectorization, including the use of sentiment lexicons and Spanish word embeddings.

  • Test_Models/ — Scripts used for model training and testing, together with the classification reports and carbon-emission reports generated during the experiments.

  • Statistical_Significance/ — Scripts and results associated with the statistical analysis of the best-performing models.

Machine learning and deep learning models

The experimental framework includes several machine learning, deep learning, and large language model approaches. The machine learning models include Support Vector Machines implemented with LinearSVC, Logistic Regression, CatBoost, and XGBoost. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was implemented using TensorFlow/Keras.

The experiments also include transformer-based models using the Hugging Face Transformers framework, specifically:

  • bert-base-multilingual-cased

  • dccuchile/bert-base-spanish-wwm-cased

  • ClassCat/roberta-base-spanish

Large language model experiments include Google's Gemini (gemini-2.0-flash) through the Google GenAI library and Meta's Llama 3.1 70B model executed locally through Ollama.

Differential Evolution optimization is implemented using scipy.optimize.differential_evolution.

External resources

The experiments rely on several third-party datasets and resources that are not redistributed with this repository. Users must obtain these resources directly from their respective original sources and comply with their applicable licenses and terms of use.

The external resources include:

  1. SemEval-2018 Task 1, Subtask E-c — Emotion Classification, Spanish dataset, used as the emotion classification corpus.

  2. ML-Senticon, used as a Spanish sentiment lexicon.

  3. SEL (Spanish Emotion Lexicon), used as an emotion-related lexical resource.

  4. Full-Strength Lexicon, used as a sentiment-related lexical resource.

  5. Spanish FastText word vectors (wiki.es.vec), used as pretrained Spanish word embeddings.

  6. Pretrained transformer models, obtained through the Hugging Face Transformers ecosystem.

  7. Gemini and Llama 3.1, accessed through their respective software interfaces and services.

  8. Syntactic n-gram extraction script, based on the MultiSngram implementation by Grigori Sidorov, used to obtain syntactic n-grams from the text corpus.

The repository provides the scripts and configuration necessary to use these resources in the experimental workflow, but does not redistribute third-party models, embeddings, datasets, or lexical resources.

Reproducibility

The experiments were implemented in Python and are intended to be executed in a Linux-based environment. Shell scripts are provided to facilitate the execution of the experimental workflow.

Users should first install Python 3.10 or later and the dependencies specified in the repository documentation. Additional external resources must then be downloaded and placed in the directories indicated in the README.txt.

Once the required dependencies and resources are available, the experimental workflow can be executed using:

bash run_tests.sh

The generated classification and carbon-emission reports are stored in:

Test_Models/output/

The repository is provided as a reproducibility resource accompanying the associated research article. Users are encouraged to cite both the original third-party resources and the associated research article when using this repository.

Authors

Luis Alberto Camacho Vázquez
Vanessa Alejandra Camacho Vázquez
Sandra Dinora Orantes Jiménez
Grigori Sidorov

metadata.title: meshlens: Serialization Order Confounds Attention Analysis in MeshXL
metadata.description: Code, preregistrations, and run artifacts showing that attention in an autoregressive 3D mesh transformer tracks the order in which the mesh was serialized rather than the geometry of the mesh itself. In MeshXL's canonical serialization a face's index in the token stream predicts its vertical position at Spearman 0.951, so attention maps painted onto a mesh surface are confounded with plain recency before any causal question is asked.

metadata.title: Thematic Observation Search, Segmentation, Collation and Analysis (TOS2CA)
metadata.description:
Thematic Observation Search, Segmentation, Collation and Analysis (TOS2CA) is a user-driven, data-centric system that identifies, collates, statistically characterizes, and serves Earth science data relevant to a given phenomenon. It facilitates the collation and analysis of data from disparate sources and makes it possible for scientists to establish science traceability requirements, quantify detection thresholds, define uncertainty requirements, and establish data sufficiency to formulate truly innovative missions and research investigations.

Version 2.2 of the software includes new features, primarily:

  • Python packaging for easier install
  • Unit testing
  • Documentation updates
  • Minor bug fixes

metadata.title: httk Extension Package for Brain and Adipose Compartments
metadata.description: The included software package provides an extension to the high-throughput toxicokinetics (httk) R package (v2.2.2). While the standard httk framework offers generalized pbtk modeling, this modification integrates specific compartments for adipose and brain tissues, following modeling framework described by Davidson-Fritz et al. (2025). The model utilizes a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) implemented through C script for computational efficiency. Key features include updated chemical-specific parameterization and the new “solve_pbtk_adipose_complexbrain” function, allowing for predictions of chemical distribution in these compartments.
